name: Retail

reading.body:
Retail AI is tracked by four independent sources covering adoption, store technology, market size, and software spend, but none of them measures the compute or power behind those systems.

The four sources form a layered measurement stack. Census BTOS updates adoption every two weeks across all sectors, including retail trade. NRF adds detail on store automation, inventory computer vision, and customer-experience software. Coresight sizes the market for merchandising and supply-chain logistics, while IHL tracks software expenditure and operational return in grocery, apparel, and general merchandise. Adoption is measured rather than guessed, and the Census series updates often enough to show change.

For AI specifically, the volume use cases are demand forecasting, recommendation, and customer-service automation. These run across many stores and transactions, so even small changes in adoption or software spend can signal where inference workloads are growing. But the data stops at adoption and spend. None of the four sources reports electricity demand, data center capacity, or compute requirements, so the data cannot support claims about grid constraints or building needs for retail AI.

summary: Demand forecasting, recommendation, and customer-service automation are the volume use cases.

analysis.body:
Retail AI adoption is measured rather than estimated. Per the Census Bureau, through its Business Trends and Outlook Survey, 16.5% of retail trade firms (NAICS 44-45) answered Yes to whether the business used AI in the last two weeks, up from 15.5% in the prior period. The series was first asked in September 2023 and is updated fortnightly, so retail sits alongside every other sector in a consistent, recurring count rather than a one-off vendor survey.

The sources describe what that spending is aimed at. IHL Group, which tracks retail technology expenditure and operational return across grocery, apparel, and general merchandise, reports that most retail AI budgets fund the wrong layer first, and that its 2026 work examines what stalls AI pilots before they reach the store floor. Its study of 96 specialty retail brands, in cooperation with Chain Store Age, finds that inventory data accuracy, not AI budget size, separates specialty retail winners from laggards. IHL also puts inventory distortion at $1.7 trillion, with empty shelves still costing $690.9 billion, and notes that AI agents no longer wait. The practical center of gravity in this material is inventory visibility and the data layer beneath it, not customer-facing novelty.

Where money and vendors concentrate is visible in the same source. IHL describes Amazon asking Meta to remove its e-commerce site from Muse, Meta's AI shopping agent, saying it did not authorize the tool's access, with Muse using Link by Stripe for purchases while Amazon's own AI-backed Buy for Me tool enables purchases from external sellers. IHL also reports Amazon expanding smart-glasses trials for delivery drivers using computer vision, AI, cameras and precision geospatial technology for walking directions, package-location assistance and hazard alerts, after 275,000 test deliveries, with plans for 5,000 additional devices and a target of 20,000 deployed by the end of 2027. Agentic commerce and store-floor computer vision are where the largest named players are placing bets.

The material also shows AI reaching smaller operators through build rather than buy. IHL reports that Castle Resorts and Hotels used AI-assisted development to launch a unified direct-booking wrapper across 20 Hawaii, Reno, and Auckland properties, with CastleResorts.com connecting five reservation systems, supporting SEO, GEO and WCAG 2.1 AA standards, and giving the operator in-house control for rapid testing and promotions. That is a hospitality example inside the retail technology research stream, and it illustrates the pattern of connecting existing systems rather than replacing them.

On the research and convening side, the National Retail Federation covers store automation, inventory computer vision, and customer-experience software, and its account of conversations in Paris describes retailers moving from practical AI to connected stores and relationship-driven loyalty. Coresight Research produces adoption rates and market sizing for AI in merchandising and supply-chain logistics, and runs an invite-only forum on AI for consumer-focused businesses. Both organizations frame the field as merchandising, supply chain, and store operations rather than a single application.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the sources point to a few things. Adoption is real but still a minority of retail firms per the Census Bureau, so the question is less whether peers are using AI than where it pays. IHL's findings suggest the constraint is usually data accuracy and pilot execution rather than budget, and that inventory visibility is the layer where returns are being measured. The regulatory posture and risk side is largely absent from these excerpts, so there is little here on compliance obligations or failure modes beyond the competitive friction visible in the Amazon and Meta dispute over agent access.

https://nrf.com/.brief: The National Retail Federation describes itself as an advocate for the people, policies, and ideas that support a thriving retail sector, and it provides retail news, insights, and industry events. According to the organization, conversations held in Paris illustrated how retailers are putting what it calls "The Next Now" into practice. These efforts span practical artificial intelligence, connected stores, and loyalty programs built on relationships.

https://coresight.com/.brief: Coresight Research describes itself as delivering data-driven insights on retail and technology, and claims a depth of expertise in China that it calls "unique in the industry." Its page also promotes a Shoptalk Fall 2026 Day 3 morning line-up, listing sessions on David's Bridal and Equinox selling past the core product, Crocs and Kenneth Cole marketing through entertainment, and Claire's and The Children's Place checking AI against the store. Coresight adds that it leads an invite-only yet collaborative forum exploring AI and the opportunities and challenges it presents for consumer-focused businesses.

https://ihlservices.com/.brief: IHL Group conducts research on retail technology spending and strategy. According to their 2026 study of 96 specialty retail brands, inventory data accuracy rather than AI budget size determines which specialty retailers succeed, and most retail AI budgets fund the wrong infrastructure layer first. The organisation also reports that inventory distortion has declined to $1.7 trillion, though empty shelves still cost $690.9 billion annually. IHL's analysis finds that the presence of AI does not predict pricing-platform quality among vendors, and retailers should instead evaluate explainability, automation controls, and governance safeguards.
